title: Sickle-cell anemia as a molecular disease
research_question: Could the abnormal red-cell phenotype in sickle-cell anemia reflect a detectable molecular difference in hemoglobin?
context: Team research culminating in the 1949 Science paper by Pauling, Itano, Singer and Wells.
known_at_the_time: Sickling was associated with oxygen conditions and red-cell behavior.
Protein/hemoglobin physicochemical differences were experimentally testable.
unknown_at_the_time: The later amino-acid-level molecular explanation and modern genetic detail.
trigger_or_anomaly: A striking cellular phenotype suggested that a molecular difference might be measurable rather than treated only as a descriptive disease category.
decision_action: Translate a phenotypic disease difference into a testable molecular comparison of hemoglobin properties, using team-based experimental work.
observed_result: The 1949 paper reported distinct electrophoretic behavior of hemoglobin associated with sickle-cell anemia/trait and framed the condition as a molecular disease.
alternative_interpretations: The experimental path and intellectual ownership were distributed across Pauling, Itano, Singer, Wells and prior clinical observations; avoid single-hero attribution.
notes: MVP team-attribution example. Add contemporaneous letters/lab records before reconstructing specific who-decided-what chronology.
